oldStep1.2: 1.2 The loop $\gamma(t)=(\cos(2\pi t),\sin(2\pi t))$ has smooth coordinate functions on all of $\mathbb R$, so its restriction to $[0,1]$ is a smooth singular one-simplex; $\gamma(0)=\gamma(1)$ and [F3] gives $\partial\gamma=0$. Pulling back gives $\gamma^*A=2\pi\,dt$, because $-y\,dx+x\,dy=2\pi\,dt$ and $x^2+y^2=1$ along $\gamma$; hence [F4] identifies $\int_\gamma A=2\pi$ as its period. If a globally defined smooth $\chi$ satisfied $A=d\chi$, then [F6] would give $\int_\gamma A=\int_\gamma d\chi=\int_{\partial\gamma}\chi=0$, contradicting this value. Thus $A$ is not globally exact. [F3, F4, F5, F6, given, algebra]
newStep1.2: 1.2 By [F9], the coordinate functions of $\gamma(t)=(\cos(2\pi t),\sin(2\pi t))$ are smooth on all of $\mathbb R$, using composition with the affine function $2\pi t$ and the chain rule in [F2]. By [F10], $\cos^2(2\pi t)+\sin^2(2\pi t)=1$, so this extension takes values in the punctured plane. It therefore supplies the neighbourhood-smooth extension required for a singular one-simplex in [F3]. The zero values in [F10] and periodicity in [F11] give $\gamma(0)=\gamma(1)=(1,0)$, hence $\partial\gamma=0$. Differentiating by [F10] and the chain rule gives $\gamma^*dx=-2\pi\sin(2\pi t)\,dt$ and $\gamma^*dy=2\pi\cos(2\pi t)\,dt$. Thus the pulled-back numerator is $2\pi(\sin^2(2\pi t)+\cos^2(2\pi t))\,dt=2\pi\,dt$, and its denominator is $1$, so $\gamma^*A=2\pi\,dt$. In the positive affine coordinate on the standard one-simplex, [F5] and [F12] reduce its integral to the rectangle integral of the constant $2\pi$ on $[0,1]$. For any partition $0=t_0<\cdots<t_m=1$, every subinterval has infimum and supremum $2\pi$, so both Darboux sums equal $\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}2\pi(t_{i+1}-t_i)=2\pi$. Their lower supremum and upper infimum therefore agree at $2\pi$, proving $\int_\gamma A=2\pi>0$ by [F11]; [F4] identifies this as the period. If a globally defined smooth $\chi$ satisfied $A=d\chi$, then [F6] would give $\int_\gamma A=\int_\gamma d\chi=\int_{\partial\gamma}\chi=0$, contradicting that positive value. Thus $A$ is not globally exact. [F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F9, F10, F11, F12, given, algebra]
addedFactsF9F12:
[F9] [[def-sine-and-cosine-by-power-series]] defines sine and cosine by their real power series; [[lem-sine-and-cosine-series-converge-everywhere]] gives infinite radius for both, and [[cor-power-series-sums-are-smooth-with-coefficient-formula]] makes their sums smooth on all of $\mathbb R$.

[F10] [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]] gives $\sin'=\cos$, $\cos'=-\sin$, $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$; [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]] gives $\sin^2u+\cos^2u=1$ for every real $u$.

[F11] [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]] gives $\pi>0$, and [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]] gives the common period $2\pi$ of sine and cosine.

[F12] [[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]] defines the Jordan-set integral by zero extension to a bounding rectangle. [[def-multidimensional-darboux-sums]] and [[def-multidimensional-darboux-integral]] define its rectangle integral by the lower and upper grid sums and their common extremal value; this includes a one-dimensional interval used as its own bounding rectangle.
